title: A complete small learning loop: fit with Adam, test beyond the training window, and check the gradient three ways
summary: A toy decay problem carries the whole workflow: a training curve, a rollout from an unseen start beyond the training time, a forward-and-backward diagram, and four ways of computing one gradient that all agree to nine digits.

media.alt: Line chart titled actual toy training, 250 Adam updates. Horizontal axis training epoch from 0 to 250, vertical axis trajectory mean squared error on a log scale from 10 to the minus 6 to 10 to the minus 3. A single orange curve oscillates and falls steeply over the first 60 epochs, then declines slowly to about 8 times 10 to the minus 7.

read_the_figure.question: Did training converge to something that works on conditions it never saw, and is the gradient the optimizer used correct?
read_the_figure.axes: Training chart: epoch (0 to 250) against trajectory MSE (log, dimensionless). Rollout chart: dimensionless time 0 to 4 against state y; a dotted vertical line at time 2 marks the end of the training window. Gradient diagram: four rows, each a method and one number.
look_at: The training curve: noisy oscillation for the first 60 epochs (the optimizer overshoots), then a smooth slow decline. The final value is about 8e-7, six orders of magnitude better than the start (about 9e-4 to 1e-3).

The rollout chart: a black reference and a dashed learned curve start at y(0) = 1.2, a value not used in training, and stay on top of each other through the dotted line, so the model works beyond the training time.
Slide 15 diagram: forward prediction, compare loss, backward sensitivity. The caption says backward credit is not reversed chemistry: it is a derivative, not an inverse simulation.
Slide 16 diagram: analytic, finite difference, direct autograd and adjoint all give 0.095925685. Four independent routes agreeing to nine digits is the test.
Check each statement against the axes: log vertical axis for loss, dimensionless units for both toy axes.
read_the_figure.proves: Loss falling by six decades shows fit, but only the rollout from an unseen start shows generalization; only an independent gradient check shows the optimizer was told the truth.
if_wrong: A loss that stalls early: learning rate too small or gradients wrong.
A rollout that departs right after the dotted line: the model memorised the training window instead of learning the rate.
Gradient methods that disagree in the third digit: a bug, or a step size in the finite difference that is too large or too small.
must_check: That the test start is not in the training set.
That the rollout extends beyond the training horizon and says where it starts.
That the gradient check lists the methods and shows enough digits.
That the loss axis is logarithmic.

terms.meaning: One pass of the optimizer updates over the data.
A gradient-based optimizer with per-parameter step sizes from running averages.
Integrating the learned rate from an initial state over a time window.
Computing the gradient of a loss through an ODE solve by integrating a second ODE backward in time.
Approximating a derivative by the change in the loss for a small change in a parameter.

remember: Fit, generalize and gradient correctness are three separate checks.
Test on an initial state and a time horizon not used in training.
A gradient is verified by comparing independent methods.
The backward pass is a derivative computation, not a run of the physics backward.

steps.title: The toy and its loss
steps.note: The simplest model with a known exact gradient; the rollout chart's reference is a decay with rate about 0.7 (read from its values).

steps.title: Exact gradient of the toy
steps.note: Chain rule on the closed form: this is the 'analytic' row of slide 16 for this toy.

steps.title: Central finite difference and its best step
steps.note: Truncation error shrinks like delta squared but round-off grows like epsilon over delta; their balance is near 6e-6 in double precision.

steps.title: Adjoint equation
steps.tex: \frac{\mathrm da}{\mathrm dt}=-a^{\mathsf T}\frac{\partial f}{\partial y},\quad a(T)=\frac{\partial L}{\partial y(T)},\quad \frac{\mathrm dL}{\mathrm d\theta}=-\int_0^T a^{\mathsf T}\frac{\partial f}{\partial\theta}\,\mathrm dt
steps.note: One extra backward solve gives the gradient with respect to all parameters at once. This is the fourth row of slide 16.

worked.title: Exact gradient of an illustrative toy
worked.problem: Take y0 = 1.2, theta = 0.7, T = 1 and a target 0.5 (illustrative values). Compute dL/dtheta.
worked.answer: About -0.114. The sign is negative: y(T) = 0.596 is above the target 0.5, so a larger rate pulls it down and lowers the loss; gradient descent would raise theta.

analyze.q: The curve oscillates for the first 60 epochs and then declines smoothly. Give one reason for each regime.
The rollout stays accurate beyond t = 2. Why does learning a rate extrapolate in time where learning a trajectory would not?
analyze.hint: The rule is the same at every time.

evaluate.q: Four gradient methods agree to nine digits. Is that sufficient evidence for a large network? What does it not test?
evaluate.hint: One parameter, one data point, one toy.

evaluate.q: Is a loss of 8e-7 on the training window a good result without the rollout figure?

create: Extend the rollout figure with a second unseen start and a start beyond the training range, and say what you expect.
Design a gradient check for a network with many parameters that costs two solves, not one per parameter.

checks.q: Why a log axis for training loss?
checks.answer: The loss falls by about six decades; a log axis shows equal factors as equal distances.

checks.q: Why is a rollout from y(0) = 1.2 a better test than one from a training start?
checks.answer: It tests the learned rate on a state not used for fitting; a training start only tests memory.

checks.q: Backward sensitivity 'is not reversed chemistry'. What would reversed chemistry mean and why is it a different thing?
checks.answer: Integrating the physics backward in time (often ill-posed); the adjoint integrates a linear sensitivity equation backward, which is well-posed.

checks.q: How would you extend the gradient check to show the failure of a finite difference step that is too small?
checks.answer: Plot the error of the finite difference against delta on log axes: a V shape with the minimum near 1e-6.
